lesson.text: Quick memory: in one-point perspective, where do the lines going away from you meet? (At one vanishing point on the horizon.) Today: the Renaissance, when artists mastered perspective, anatomy and light.
Renaissance means rebirth. From about 1400 to 1600, starting in Florence in Italy, artists and thinkers looked again at ancient Greek and Roman art. And they studied the world closely.

Linear perspective: Filippo Brunelleschi (1377-1446) showed how it works in Florence about 1415. Masaccio (1401-1428) used it in his Holy Trinity, about 1427, so a flat wall seemed to open into a chapel.

Raphael (1483-1520) painted The School of Athens (1509-1511). Follow the floor tiles and the arches: they all lead to one vanishing point between the two thinkers in the middle, so your eye goes straight to them.

Anatomy: Renaissance artists studied how bodies are built, bones and muscles, to draw them in proportion. Leonardo da Vinci (1452-1519) drew the Vitruvian Man: arms spread out are as wide as the man is tall.
Light: chiaroscuro means light-dark. Strong light and deep shadow make forms look solid. Leonardo also used sfumato, soft smoky edges with no hard lines, in the Mona Lisa, begun in 1503.

In the north, Jan van Eyck (about 1390-1441) used oil paint in thin see-through layers for glowing colour and fine detail. See the Arnolfini Portrait (1434). Michelangelo (1475-1564) carved the marble David (1501-1504), over 5 m tall.
Try it in the world: draw a hallway in one-point perspective, light it from one window, and shade it with strong chiaroscuro. Next: colour harmony.

exercises.hint: Think of what artists looked back to: the art of ancient Greece and Rome.
exercises.explain: Renaissance means rebirth: ancient Greek and Roman ideas were born again.

exercises.prompt: In which city did the Renaissance begin?
exercises.hint: Brunelleschi and Masaccio worked there, in Italy.
exercises.explain: It began in Florence, in Italy, about 1400.

exercises.prompt: In linear perspective, lines going away from you meet at a vanishing point.
exercises.hint: Think of railway lines going into the distance.
exercises.explain: True: parallel lines that go away from you seem to meet at one point on the horizon.

exercises.prompt: Match each word to its meaning.
exercises.hint: Chiaro means light and scuro dark; fumo means smoke.
exercises.explain: perspective: depth; anatomy: bodies; chiaroscuro: light and dark; sfumato: smoky; fresco: wet plaster.

exercises.hint: He also drew the Vitruvian Man.
exercises.explain: Leonardo da Vinci began it in 1503.

exercises.prompt: Where do the lines of the floor and the arches meet?
exercises.hint: Follow two orange lines with your finger until they cross.
choices: between the two thinkers in the middle
exercises.explain: They meet at the vanishing point between the two thinkers, so the eye goes to them.

exercises.prompt: In the Vitruvian Man, the arm span is about as wide as the man is tall.
exercises.hint: Look at the square round him.
exercises.explain: True: arms out, he fits a square, as tall as he is wide.

exercises.prompt: Which technique makes soft, smoky edges with no hard lines?
exercises.explain: Sfumato, as round the Mona Lisa's eyes and mouth.

exercises.prompt: Sort the artists into where they worked.
exercises.hint: Van Eyck worked in Flanders and Dürer in Germany.
exercises.explain: Leonardo, Raphael and Michelangelo worked in Italy; van Eyck and Dürer in the north.

exercises.prompt: Michelangelo painted the Sistine Chapel ceiling from 1508 to 1512. How many years is that?
exercises.hint: Take the first year from the last.
exercises.explain: 1512 − 1508 = 4 years, much of it lying on his back on scaffolding.

exercises.prompt: Oil paint could be laid on in thin, see-through layers, giving glowing colours.
exercises.hint: Think of Jan van Eyck's paintings.
exercises.explain: True: thin glazes of oil paint let light shine through them.

exercises.prompt: Put these in time order, the earliest first.
exercises.hint: Masaccio died young in 1428; the Sistine ceiling was finished in 1512.
items: Van Eyck paints the Arnolfini Portrait

exercises.prompt: Why did Renaissance artists study anatomy?
exercises.hint: What were they trying to paint better?
choices: to draw bodies in proportion and pose them well
exercises.explain: Knowing the bones and muscles under the skin helped them draw bodies that look real.

exercises.prompt: What does chiaroscuro do to a painting?
exercises.hint: Think of strong light on one side and deep shadow on the other.
exercises.explain: Strong light and dark model the forms, so they look solid and three-dimensional.

exercises.prompt: Leonardo was born in 1452. How many years later, in 1503, did he start the Mona Lisa?
In The School of Athens, why are the two thinkers in the middle easy to notice?
choices: every line leads the eye to them
exercises.explain: The perspective lines all lead to the vanishing point between them: the eye follows.

exercises.prompt: Match each artwork to the Renaissance idea it shows best.
exercises.hint: Think of lines meeting at a point, a body in a square, soft edges, and glowing colour.
exercises.explain: Raphael's School of Athens leads every line to one vanishing point: perspective. Leonardo's Vitruvian Man studies the body's proportions. The Mona Lisa's soft edges are sfumato. Van Eyck's Arnolfini Portrait glows with thin oil layers.
